summary: Explains why the DNS Server and Resolver MIB extensions were never deployed after six years as proposed standards, and recommends retiring them by moving them to Historical status.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo explains why two proposed DNS management extensions were never deployed. It recommends moving their RFCs to Historic status and offers lessons for future work.

questions: why were dns mib extensions not deployed
which dns mib rfc numbers does it address
subtitle: Why the DNS Server and Resolver MIB extensions were not deployed and should be retired.

tldr.problem: The DNS Server and Resolver MIB extensions remained undeployed after more than six years as Proposed Standards.
tldr.mechanism: The memo reviews design and implementation problems and recommends reclassifying RFCs 1611 and 1612 as Historic.
tldr.outcome: It records lessons about setting clear goals, limiting scope, and choosing a suitable management framework.

today: RFC 3197 recommends reclassifying RFC 1611 and RFC 1612 as Historic because the extensions were not deployed.

sections.title: Why the DNS MIB Work Stalled
sections.content:
The author says the working group lacked agreement about what the DNS MIB extensions should contain. The work began during a period when many protocols were receiving MIB extensions, without enough attention to the goal the DNS work should serve.

The extensions grew large and often matched counters in a particular BIND version. Attempts to make them implementation-neutral did not prevent new variables from closely tracking BIND statistics.
sections.plainLanguage: The project did not begin with a clear agreement about what users needed. Its scope grew, and parts remained tied to one DNS implementation.

sections.title: Technical and Implementation Barriers
sections.content:
The memo says the SMI was not well suited to some DNS management needs. For example, direct indexing into large resolver caches required complex clauses and ran into known object-identifier length limits in some SNMP implementations.

The lack of SNMP proxy MIB support and a standard subagent protocol also made implementation in BIND difficult. AgentX later became viable, but by then the author says interest in implementing the extensions had faded.
sections.plainLanguage: The management framework made some DNS data difficult to represent. Missing support in the dominant implementation added another barrier.

sections.title: Lessons and Recommendation
sections.content:
The RFC advises future efforts to define goals and their intended users first, keep MIB extensions short, and avoid adding measurements without a clear need. It also says that difficulty fitting a task into the SMI may indicate that SNMP is the wrong tool.

Given the apparent lack of interest in deployment, the author recommends reclassifying RFCs 1611 and 1612 as Historic. The memo says this should not harm Internet security and should not create IANA work.
sections.plainLanguage: Start with a clear problem, keep the design focused, and choose a tool that fits. The author recommends Historic status for the two extensions.
